@@120004021 <p> Think you know everything about flying ? Buckle up ! We 're about to take a high-altitude dip into 12 astounding aviation facts that will give you a whole new perspective on what happens above the clouds . From why 80% of people have never flown to how planes can trigger lightning , get ready for a fascinating journey through the skies ! <h> You are less likely to die from flying than from walking <p> Flying is widely regarded as the safest mode of transport , significantly safer than driving . According to the International Air Transport Association ( IATA ) , the all-accident rate was just 0.80 per million flights in 2023 , an all-time low and a significant improvement from the 1.30 rate in 2022 . This performance is better than the five-year average of 1.19 . <p> To put this in perspective , consider that in the United States alone , 7,522 pedestrians were fatally injured in traffic incidents in 2022 . However , 2024 saw a shift , with 318 fatalities in aircraft accidents , marking it the deadliest year in aviation since 2018 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of people have never flown <p> While a small group of frequent flyers dominates the skies , most of the world remains earthbound . About 90% of people globally do not take even a single flight each year . A staggering 80% of the world 's population has never flown at all . The reasons range from the prohibitive costs and fears of flying to a deliberate choice to avoid air travel to combat climate change . <h> The most expensive flight ticket was $123,000 <p> In 2007 , Julian Hayward , an Australian millionaire , set the record for the highest price ever paid for a flight ticket -- $123,000 . He secured his place in history by winning an auction for two seats on the inaugural flight of the Airbus A380 from Singapore to Sydney . This was n't just any ticket ; it was a charitable contribution that got him aboard the largest passenger plane ever built at the time . <h> 1 in 20 bags go missing ( 1.8 million in 2023 ) <p> In 2023 , the issue of misplaced luggage continued to plague air @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This equates to about one mishandled bag for every 20 checked . The problem was particularly acute on international routes , where the likelihood of losing luggage was five times higher than domestic flights . However , the SITA Baggage IT Insights Report highlights an improvement over 2022 , with the rate of lost , delayed , or damaged luggage dropping to 6.9 per 1,000 passengers from a higher rate of 7.6 the previous year . <h> Chicken carcasses are fired at aircraft for safety checks <p> Did you know that chicken guns have been crucial to aviation safety since the 1940s ? These compressed-air cannons are designed to launch chicken carcasses at high speeds to simulate bird strikes on aircraft engines and windshields . <p> This unique testing ensures that aircraft can withstand these mid-air collisions , a critical factor in certification regulations . While the concept might sound a bit bizarre , it 's a vital practice in the industry . Most airlines do n't own these devices and prefer to use specialized facilities to conduct these essential safety tests . <h> Back seats are your best bets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where you should sit on a plane for maximum safety ? According to a detailed analysis by Time , the rear third of an airplane might be your safest option . Crash data shows that the fatality rate for seats in the back is about 32% , significantly lower compared to other areas . In contrast , the plane 's middle section , often bustling with activity , holds the highest risk , with a fatality rate of 39% . The front section , typically coveted for its legroom and quick exit access , is slightly riskier than the back , with a fatality rate of 38% . <h> In flight , you are only 12% closer to space <p> While flying might make you feel on top of the world , commercial planes only reach a fraction of the way to outer space . The official boundary , known as the Karman Line , is 100 km ( about 330,000 feet ) above Earth . Most commercial airliners cruise at altitudes between 30,000 and 40,000 feet which is roughly 12% of the distance to space . Even the legendary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ascend to 60,000 feet , just over 18% of the way to the Karman Line . So , while we soar high , we 're still far from venturing into the cosmos on regular flights . <h> Pointing a laser at planes could get you 5 years in prison <p> Did you know that pointing a laser pointer at an aircraft is dangerous and a serious federal offense ? The seemingly harmless act of aiming that irritating red dot at a jet can have severe legal consequences . According to 18 U.S. Code Section 39A , anyone caught intentionally targeting an aircraft with a laser could face up to five years in prison . <h> Commercial planes can fly with a single engine <p> Modern airplanes are designed to handle engine failures gracefully . Commercial aircraft , like the Boeing Dreamliner , are certified to fly with just one engine for up to 330 minutes , enough to cross vast oceans or remote areas safely . Even more impressively , planes like the Boeing 747 can glide for miles if all engines fail , thanks to their optimal glide ratios @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , even in the most challenging situations . <h> Airplane trails are just water vapor <p> Have you ever noticed those white lines crisscrossing the sky behind an airplane ? Those are contrails , short for condensation trails , formed by the water vapor released during the combustion process in plane engines . As the hot vapor exits the exhaust , it encounters the cooler , high-altitude air , condensing into visible ice crystals . This phenomenon is akin to seeing your breath on a cold day -- simple , yet fascinating science at work in the skies . <h> Airplanes can trigger lightning <p> Airplanes can inadvertently trigger lightning when flying through charged clouds . Despite the dramatic nature of a strike , the risk to passengers is minimal due to advanced aircraft design . With their conductive aluminum bodies and grounded electrical systems , commercial airplanes are built to disperse electrical energy safely . Each plane is struck by lightning about once a year on average , yet there has been no major incident caused by lightning in the U.S. since 1967 , thanks to these robust safety @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Contrary to their name , airplane black boxes are bright orange , a feature that aids in their recovery after an accident . These crucial devices comprise two main components , the Flight Data Recorder ( FDR ) and the Cockpit Voice Recorder ( CVR ) . The FDR carefully logs various flight parameters , while the CVR captures all cockpit conversations and sounds . Blackboxes are instrumental in solving the mysteries behind aviation incidents and provide key insights that help improve future flight safety . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint . <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Kaif Shaikh Kaif Shaikh is a journalist and writer passionate about turning complex information into clear , impactful stories . @@120004646 <h> Phase-changing crystals could cut air-conditioning 's climate impact <p> Materials commonly used in batteries can exchange large amounts of heat with the atmosphere when they undergo a pressure-induced phase transition . The effect might mean that organic ionic plastic crystals could find a second use enabling highly-efficient cooling without a refrigerant -- dramatically reducing the carbon footprint of air-conditioning in a warming world . <p> The organic ionic plastic crystals undergo a pressure-induced phase transition that causes them to give out or take in heat <p> Current air-conditioning technology based on vapour compression contributes to climate change in two ways . The first comes from powering the device : air conditioning and electric fans already account for around 10% of global electricity consumption . The second is from the refrigerants -- greenhouse gases sometimes thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide . ' We know that there 's significant leakage of those materials into the environment , ' says materials scientist Jenny Pringle at Deakin University in Victoria , Australia . Refrigerant-free alternatives to vapour compression could erase the second contribution , but if they were less energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ materials give out or take in heat when an applied stimulus such as an electric or magnetic field causes them to transition between two solid phases with different entropy . This can then be used to transfer heat from cold to hot . Studies suggest this solid-state refrigeration could potentially be more energy efficient than vapour compression . <p> The barocaloric effect utilises pressure to trigger the phase transition . When a material transitions to a low-entropy , ordered state on compression , heat is released to the environment . If the pressure is released and it returns to a disordered state , the material once again takes in heat . The thermal energy exchange can be much larger than in other caloric effects , but the materials with the largest barocaloric effects discovered to date remain in the ordered state at ambient temperature and pressure , which makes them unsuitable for cooling . ' There are some other materials that have transitions below room temperature and there are other materials that have large barocaloric effects , but there are not a lot of materials that display both , ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the organic ionic plastic crystals studied by Pringle and her colleagues <p> Pringle and her colleagues studied organic ionic plastic crystals , which were known to have a high-energy phase transition to a disordered ionic structure at low temperatures . This has been exploited to produce highly conductive electrolytes for sodium and lithium ion batteries . ' It turns out the intrinsic material properties that make them good for that also make them good for barocalorics , ' says Pringle . <p> The researchers established that some existing crystals showed extremely promising properties , and they are now investigating why these examples are particularly promising and hope to design new , hopefully even better ones . <p> ' I think this is a really important step , ' says materials scientist Mengfan Guo at the University of Cambridge , UK . He notes two especially important points . First , the transition temperature is not just below room temperature but actually below freezing in some cases , which could allow calorics to be used in freezers . Secondly , he says that , although the materials do not present record @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to further exploration of a wide family of materials that industry can already produce fairly cheaply for battery applications . ' That 's pretty exciting , ' he says .

It was the considered action of a responsible citizen acting out of conscience . In the face of the permanent collapse of our climate , our economy , our society and life on Earth , the only thing that keeps me going is our continued capacity as people to care , regardless of what happens . Yes , I fear prison , but I am ready to go if I must . " <h> Implications of the climate crisis for the medical profession <p> Dr Hart now faces a hearing with the Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service ( MPTS ) , where he could potentially have his medical license suspended or be struck off the register entirely . This development follows similar cases where doctors have faced professional repercussions for climate activism . Notably , retired GPs Dr Sarah Benn and Dr Diana Warner were suspended after convictions related to environmental protests . <p> The General Medical Council ( GMC ) has stated that while doctors have the right to express their opinions , unlawful actions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it 's the act of breaking the law , not the motivation behind it , that is subject to disciplinary action . <p> Dr Hart told the court he feared prison but accepted the consequences of his protest when compared to not acting at all . " <h> A wider movement <p> Dr Hart is among a growing number of professionals -- including teachers , care workers and students -- who have faced legal consequences for climate activism . His imprisonment underscores the increasing tensions between activists , authorities and protest policing and sentencing amid worsening climate breakdown . Dr Patrick Hart 's sentencing is more than a legal judgment ; it 's a reflection of the broader societal struggle to address the climate emergency . His case challenges us to consider the lengths to which individuals -- and professionals bound by ethical codes -- should go in advocating for the planet 's future . <p> As the climate crisis intensifies , the actions of Dr Hart and others may well inspire a reevaluation of professional responsibilities and the role of civil disobedience in effecting change . <p> Dr Rita Issa is a GP and academic researching climate change and health . She is the co-editor of the upcoming book Health , Resistance and Activism.

Trees play a pivotal role in mitigating climate change , preserving biodiversity , and enhancing human health by improving air quality and providing mental health benefits . This interconnection underscores the urgency of protecting our trees to ensure environmental resilience and societal well-being for future generations . <p> Ireland has one of the lowest levels of forest cover in Europe , with just 11.6% of its land area covered by trees , compared to a European average of 40% . Despite this , trees have long held a profound significance in Ireland 's landscape , culture , and ecosystems . Among them , the ash tree ( Fraxinus excelsior ) -- in Irish fuinse ? g -- stands as a cornerstone of biodiversity and Irish culture . However , the ongoing threat of ash dieback disease , caused by invasive fungal pathogen -- Hymenoscyphus fraxineus , raises urgent questions about our responsibility to protect native trees and , with them , the future @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ native trees <p> Ireland 's native trees play crucial ecological roles , providing food and habitat to countless species . The ash tree alone supports nearly 1,000 species , including insects , mammals , bryophytes , and lichens . While many species can adapt to other trees , some are entirely dependent on ash . Losing ash trees would therefore disrupt entire ecosystems , affecting pollinators , birds , and other wildlife . <p> We need your consent to load this rte-player contentWe use rte-player to manage extra content that can set cookies on your device and collect data about your activity . Its flexibility and strength famously make it the wood of choice for crafting hurleys . Place names and local traditions across Ireland further illustrate its embeddedness @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the threat of ash dieback <p> Ash dieback is decimating ash populations across Europe , including Ireland . First detected here in 2012 , the disease spreads through airborne spores and infects trees via leaf litter . It causes leaf wilting , crown dieback , and root rot , ultimately leading to death . Young ash trees are more susceptible , with mortality rates nearing 100% in some areas . <p> Signs of the disease are now evident in Irish hedgerows , where skeletal ash trees with barren tips are becoming increasingly common . The impact is significant to that of the Dutch elm disease ( DED ) , which wiped out elms across Ireland and Europe . <p> We need your consent to load this YouTube contentWe use YouTube to manage extra content that can set cookies on your device and collect data about your activity . Once a common sight in Ireland , mature elms are now rare , with only a small number of survivors scattered across the country . <p> Efforts are underway to restore elms through breeding programmes focused on disease-tolerant varieties , such as those led by Teagasc in Ireland . This loss parallels the current challenges facing ash trees due to ash dieback disease , highlighting the importance of safeguarding native trees for biodiversity and cultural heritage . <h> Lessons for the future <p> Ash dieback underscores the risks associated with low genetic and structural diversity in forests . Many Irish ash plantations are even-aged ( where all trees are of the same age ) , which makes them more vulnerable to diseases like ash dieback . Building resilient forests requires embracing close-to-nature forestry principles that promote mixed-species woodlands , diverse tree ages , and genetic variety . <p> Mixed forests ( forests with a variety of tree species ) not only support greater biodiversity but also create ecosystems better equipped to withstand environmental pressures , including diseases and climate change . By prioritising these strategies , Irish forestry @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> The AshForFuture project <p> Despite the challenges posed by ash dieback , there is hope through scientific research and conservation efforts . Since 2015 , Teagasc has led an ash-breeding program to develop disease-tolerant genotypes . Early research has shown that up to 10% of ash trees have some tolerance to the disease , with 1-3% showing a high level of tolerance . This resistance , controlled by multiple heritable genes , provides the foundation for breeding programmes focused on producing tolerant ash genotypes . <p> As part of this work , a trial of 1,000 Irish ash genotypes was established in Lithuania , a region with high disease pressure , to identify highly tolerant trees . Additionally , Teagasc has created gene-banks , including one comprising of 208 ash genotypes from 15 European countries . Preliminary results from these trials in Ireland show promising levels of tolerance : approximately 28% of genotypes display good tolerance , and 5% exhibit a higher level of tolerance , with no signs of dieback . <p> We need your consent to load this rte-player contentWe use rte-player to manage extra content @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about your activity . Through partnerships with organisations such as Coillte , None-So-Hardy Nurseries , the Office of Public Works , and international researchers , provide additional support for this critical research . This focuses on identifying and propagating disease-tolerant trees while safeguarding the genetic diversity of Ireland 's native ash . @@120047275 <p> A new cooling innovation developed by scientists pumps away heat continuously using layers of flexing thin films . The design is based on the electrocaloric effect , in which an electric field causes a temporary change in a material 's temperature , according to researchers . <p> Developed by UCLA materials scientists , the prototype could lower ambient temperatures of its immediate surroundings by 16 degrees Fahrenheit continuously and up to 25 degrees at the source of the heat after about 30 seconds during lab experiments . <p> Qibing Pei , a professor of materials science and engineering at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering , stated that their long-term goal is to develop this technology for wearable cooling accessories that are comfortable , affordable , reliable and energy-efficient -- especially for people who work in very hot environments over long hours . <h> Material is composed of a circular stack of six thin polymer films <p> " As average temperatures continue to rise with climate change , coping with heat is becoming a critical health issue . We need a variety of solutions to the problem and this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Scientists revealed that the experimental material is composed of a circular stack of six thin polymer films , just under an inch in diameter and one-quarter of an inch thick for the entire stack . Each layer is coated with carbon nanotubes on both sides . The resulting material is ferroelectric , which means it changes shape when an electric field is applied . <p> When the device 's electric field is switched on , the stacked layers compress against each other in pairs . When the electricity switches off , the stacked pairs come apart to then press against the other neighboring layers . As this alternating process repeats itself , the self-regenerative , accordion-like cascading action continually pumps heat away , layer by layer , according to a press release . <h> Polymer films use a circuit to shuttle charges <p> Hanxiang Wu , one of the study 's co-lead authors and a postdoctoral scholar working in Pei 's lab , stated that the polymer films use a circuit to shuttle charges between pairs of stacked layers , which makes the flexible cooling device more efficient @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ technology relies on air conditioning and refrigeration , which require vapor compression that not only consumes a great deal of energy but also uses carbon dioxide as a coolant . The new device is a simpler design that does not require **25;361;TOOLONG coolants or liquids . It operates solely with electricity , which can be sustainable when generated through renewable energy sources such as solar panels , as per the release . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> Wenzhong Yan , a postdoctoral scholar in mechanical engineering , stated that this cooling device integrates advanced materials with an elegant mechanical architecture to deliver energy-efficient cooling by embedding functionality directly into its structure , reducing complexity , energy use and computational demands . <p> Pei highlighted that electrocaloric cooling would be most-ideal for next-generation wearables that can keep us cool under strenuous conditions . " It could also be used to cool electronics with flexible components , " said Pei . <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint . <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Prabhat Ranjan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Mass Communication , is a tech and defense journalist . @@120047304 <h> " Hard to comprehend " : Screen 's LA team reflect on their own experiences of the devastating wildfires <p> Look to the skies above Los Angeles on most days and you 're treated to a vista of brilliant blue . It 's a skyline that has long filled people with hope in a city of dreamers . <p> That all changed last week , when the heavens were daubed with angry purple and black clouds blocking out the sun , like a crude child 's drawing . <p> On Tuesday , January 7 , the Palisades and Eaton fires erupted , changing the lives of Angelinos forever . Residents were being ordered to evacuate the upscale Pacific Palisades suburb and the middle-class enclave of Altadena near Pasadena . In all likelihood , lives were already being lost , although this would not come to light for several days . <p> In these two suburbs that have borne the brunt of the unfolding crisis , as well as in others that have burned in the Greater Los Angeles area , carpets of flames rolled and leapt through homes , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their way . <p> Nobody still knows for sure what started these blazes . What we do know is that the initial sparks combined with dry brush that had not been rained on for months and the relentless Santa Ana winds that usually blow through in late autumn to consume communities that had thrived for decades . <p> Within hours , large swaths of Los Angeles were engulfed in a hellish landscape that was hard to comprehend . Firefighters ran towards nature 's ferocity as residents fled the other way . Bulldozers smashed through abandoned cars on gridlocked streets to make way for emergency services . People ran down Sunset Boulevard towards the Pacific Ocean , pets clutched to their chests . Structures groaned and collapsed . <p> By late last week , we were told that the rapidly spreading conflagrations were already among the worst in California 's history of wildfires , a dispiriting track record of environmental catastrophe Frankensteined in recent years by climate change . <p> On previous occasions , relatives in the UK would call , scared by news reports of fires in the vicinity when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Not this time . <p> Last Wednesday evening , the Sunset Fire took hold in the Hollywood Hills . My colleague and Screen 's president of North America , Nigel Daly , lives there , and in those frantic minutes as he , his wife and two grown-up children evacuated their home , they barely had time to reflect on the quilt of a life patched together through treasured belongings both mundane and exotic . Folders of the family history in India , signed artworks from friends , rare books , children 's mementoes -- all were bundled into the car as they drove down the hill to the safety of a friend 's house , beneath the sickening rictus of the orange glow from fires in the neighbouring canyon . <p> " As we went through our cupboards where things had been stored we discovered so much we forgot was there , " Nigel told me days later . " It brought me to tears as I realised had I lost my home , this history would have been lost too . " <p> Less than two miles south @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Hollywood sign . Residents where I live in Mid-City stood in the street , murmuring anxiously . Some were already packing bags . I had packed my car with essentials the day before -- clothes for a week , water bottles , important documents . Our apartment was not in an evacuation zone but on Thursday , as a steady drizzle of ash covered cars and authorities issued red flag warnings across the city , my partner was out of town and I drove the children to Palm Springs . My eldest has asthma and we needed to get to clean air for the weekend . <h> Tragedy and impact <p> The world 's press has written much about celebrities who have lost their homes and while that is tragic , the vast majority of those who live in the Greater Los Angeles area are not household names . Many work in the entertainment industry , and many more do not : they are our teachers , doctors and nurses , rideshare drivers , librarians , shop workers , hairdressers , small business owners ... the list goes on . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ones . We have cars , escape options . We also now have dear friends who have lost homes . Nigel 's artist friends have lost lifetimes of work . My daughter 's school went up in flames and was severely damaged . Students across the region are being relocated to new schools . <p> We continued working as best we could . The fires had triggered contingency plans in Hollywood . Television productions and at least one studio film production -- Disney 's The Hand That Rocks The Cradle -- were halted . <p> The Academy and other awards organisers postponed nominations announcements , and studios , streamers and other entertainment organisations and individuals have donated tens of millions of dollars to relief and recovery efforts . Sales agents here say packaging has been slow as they focus on more pressing personal matters . <p> Reports estimate that more than 180,000 have fled their homes . Twenty-four people are believed to have lost their lives , with officials warning that the number will grow . People are missing . There is looting . Police have blocked off roads to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ who can prove they live -- or lived -- there . <p> Inevitably , the tragedy has become a political football as the blame game and inquests into empty fire hydrants and slashed fire department budgets begin . President-elect Donald Trump has branded the region 's Democratic leaders incompetent . From afar . As of Tuesday , he did not appear to have accepted California Governor Gavin Newsom 's invitation to tour the devastation . <p> I drove back into Los Angeles on Monday and the air was eerily clear . The same on Tuesday , although by the afternoon high winds forecast for the previous night were expected to return . The National Weather Service warned that while the gusts would not be as ferocious as last week , the potential for rapid fire growth remains . <p> Nigel was back in his home the day after evacuating and spent much of Sunday trimming trees and overhanging branches , clearing footpaths in preparation for firefighters to gain access should the need arise . <p> Watch Duty is a name that was perhaps unfamiliar to many Angelinos before January 7 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by a non-profit has become a vital resource , providing real-time updates on the fires and the progress of firefighters . We keep the app on our phones close to hand . Electronics need to be fully charged , cars filled with fuel , which sounds dangerous given the circumstances but is necessary in case we are told to evacuate . <p> By Tuesday evening , Cal Fire , the state 's department of forestry and fire protection , estimated that the Palisades Fire had claimed 23,713 acres and has been 18% contained . Eaton is burning up 14,117 acres and has been 35% contained . The other smaller fires are largely contained . More than 12,300 structures have been destroyed . <p> A city with a reputation for storytelling now has thousands of new tales of woe . The broader Los Angeles economy will be severely impacted . Dreams dashed ; the soul-destroying prospect for many of insurance claims that will take months if not years ; higher asking prices that border on price-gouging ; developers and private equity waiting in the wings . For some , the monetary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ high . <p> The city is resilient and will build itself back up . But for now , the eyes of Angelinos are looking to the sky again , hoping the winds and the sickly daytime sun shrouded in smoke and bruised clouds stay away , willing these nightmare infernos to end . <h> Subscribe to Screen International <p> Screen International is the essential resource for the international film industry . @@120091372 <h> Rewilding : A meaningful response to tackling the biodiversity crisis <h> The concept is an eco-centric approach which is nature-led and human-enabled <p> Rewilding means ' giving nature the space and time to dictate its own ecological trajectory ' . Photograph : Padraic Fogarty <p> P ? draic Fogarty <p> Thu Jan 16 2025 - 06:00 <p> A decade ago , the concept of rewilding captured the public imagination as a response to the growing seriousness of the climate and biodiversity crisis . The word seemed to encapsulate not only what needs to be done , but where it has all gone wrong ; after all , we live in a world that has been " dewilded " . <p> The word " rewilding " originated in the United States in the 1980s , used by conservationists concerned with the ' three Cs ' -- cores , corridors and carnivores -- but it has since taken on meaning in the popular lexicon as pretty much anything that might give nature a boost . Media references to rewilding include everything from planting trees and bee-friendly gardening to more traditional forms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ those which are invasive . <p> Rewilding has also been subject to a backlash . Early proponents of the idea walked back their support as opposition grew from certain quarters . Rewilding was portrayed as no different from land abandonment , while its emphasis on self-sustaining ecosystems irked those who feel that human management is , and always will be , needed in order for biodiversity to flourish . For some , it was an emphasis on carnivore reintroduction that made it untouchable , believing such ideas have no place in long-domesticated landscapes like Ireland . <p> Many conservationists demurred . Rewilding means nothing , offers nothing new , is not applicable to us given our history and landscape and is a word best avoided lest it antagonise those whose support is needed if we are to reverse the growing tide of extinction . Rewilding has even been accused of being " anti-people " . <p> All of this , however , overlooks the fact that rewilding is a concept not only founded in ecological science but one that is also now firmly rooted in approaches , academic as well @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ milestone came in 2021 with the publication of 10 " guiding principles for rewilding " by a group of 33 academics in the peer-reviewed journal Conservation Biology . <p> In this paper , the authors also proposed a definition of rewilding as " the process of rebuilding , following major human disturbance , a natural ecosystem by restoring natural processes and the complete or near complete food web at all trophic levels as a self-sustaining and resilient ecosystem with biota species that would have been present had the disturbance not occurred " . The paper emphasised this would require a " paradigm shift in the relationship between humans and nature " . <p> Steve Carver is professor of rewilding and wilderness science at the school of geography in the University of Leeds , UK , and was lead author of the aforementioned paper . He is also director of the Wildland Research Institute and co-chair of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature 's rewilding thematic group . <p> He says that in many respects the science of rewilding is " still in its infancy " , but that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and time to dictate its own ecological trajectory . It 's not based on some predetermined outcome , on what we want things to look like . There 's a distinction there to be made between rewilding and ecological restoration , where you could say that all rewilding is restoration but that not all restoration is rewilding " . <p> This points to one of the more persistent debates in this topic , as the field of ecological restoration has its own history , corpus of published research and institutional bodies , leading many to claim that rewilding has nothing additional to offer . Indeed , a number of analyses have been carried out into their differences and there can be little doubt that there is substantial overlap . <p> A mature oak tree covered with moss and other plant species on the Beara Peninsula , near Eyeries , West Cork . Photograph : Paulo Nunes dos Santos/The New York Times <p> One study , published this year , concluded " the goals of ecological restoration and rewilding have a common scope : the recovery of ecosystems following anthropogenic degradation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and not in competition with one another . An example might be where worked out peatlands in the midlands are being rewetted . This will not restore the raised bog habitat that was there before industrial excavation as the damage has been too extensive . But , by repairing the hydrology , it is kick-starting ecological processes such as carbon storage while allowing new habitats to develop under their own steam . There is no defined end point . This is rewilding . <p> You 're looking at an approach where you 're trying to minimise as much as possible all human intervention and management ... and you 're looking at self-organising ; the philosophy that nature knows best <p> -- Nathalie Pettorelli <p> Carver stresses that any approach needs to be " context specific " . He is adamant that rewilding does bring something new to the party . " Ecological restoration is human-led , nature-enabled . Us deciding what we want nature to do ... whereas rewilding is more of an eco-centric approach which is nature-led and human-enabled . " <p> This eco-centric approach may be where rewilding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that nature should not be allowed to get ' out of control ' or that land should ' go wild ' has deep roots . Nevertheless , in challenging this mindset , rewilding has identified one of the leading drivers of biodiversity loss : humanity 's seeming inability to see healthy natural ecosystems as anything more than wasteland . <p> Carver says that he 's not happy that the word rewilding has been " hijacked " by some initiatives that he does not believe qualify ( he says the idea you can rewild your lawn by not mowing is " nonsense " ) , but " it is here to stay and has very much found a home in Europe " . <p> This sentiment is echoed by Prof Nathalie Pettorelli at the Zoological Society of London and co-editor of the book Rewilding ( Cambridge University Press , 2019 ) in which she wrote that rewilding represents a " transformative approach to conserving biodiversity " . <p> She tells me that " what 's different about it is that you 're looking at re-establishing natural processes . What you 're @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ been degraded in a situation where they 're getting more ecologically complex , which means more interaction between species , more self-sustaining ... so you 're looking at an approach where you 're trying to minimise as much as possible all human intervention and management ... and you 're looking at self-organising ; the philosophy that nature knows best " . <p> Pettorelli says rewilding met early resistance within the academic community , with some refusing to use the word , but since then it has become established . " Rewilding can help to identify key questions around how you tackle degradation , how you recover nature , the pros and cons of various approaches , " she says . <p> Much of the debate has centred on nailing down an accepted definition , something Pettorelli believes still needs more work . " Trying to define rewilding as something that enables something to be what it should have been if the disturbance was n't there is really not helpful in the context of climate change . " Nevertheless , she says today it 's much clearer than it was . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so easy to understand what people were talking about . Now , most people are familiar with the term and know the big principle that characterises rewilding . " <p> Like Carver , she stresses that we need to foster a range of approaches : " I do n't think we just need to do rewilding and nothing else . @@120091599 <p> During an April 2024 flyover of Greenland , NASA researchers made a startling discovery -- a vast network of tunnels hidden beneath a hundred feet of ice . At first , they had no idea what they were seeing . " We were mapping the ice bed , and out pops Camp Century , " remarked Alex Gardner , a NASA cryospheric scientist . <p> This once top-secret US military base , built at the height of the Cold War , contained an even more covert mission -- storing nuclear missiles in Arctic tunnels . What remains now is an abandoned relic brimming with hazardous waste , locked in the ice but not necessarily out of danger . As Greenland 's ice melts , the ghosts of Camp Century may soon resurface , threatening both the environment and international relations . <p> Read further or view our video to unravel the science , secrecy , and environmental implications of Camp Century 's looming return . <h> Project ice worm and hidden history under Greenland 's ice <p> Constructed in 1959 by the US Army Corps of Engineers , Camp @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Spanning 21 underground tunnels and covering 9,800 feet , this base was situated in one of Earth 's most extreme environments , with temperatures dropping to -70 ? F and winds surpassing 120 mph . <p> Initially publicized as a research facility , Camp Century also secretly housed Project Iceworm , an ambitious Cold War scheme to store nuclear missiles within ice tunnels for potential strikes against the Soviet Union . However , the ice 's dynamic and unstable nature rendered the project impractical , leading to the base 's decommissioning in 1967 and abandoning approximately 47,000 gallons of radioactive waste . <p> This waste and further details of Project Iceworm remained obscured until 1995 when a Danish foreign policy inquiry , prompted by Denmark 's Parliament following revelations about a 1968 B52 crash at Thule Airbase , brought them to light . These revelations contradicted previous claims by the government , sparking intense scrutiny over the historical management of nuclear materials in Greenland . <p> The controversy deepened in 1997 when Denmark released documents that detailed the US Army 's plans for Iceworm , outlined in the 1960 report @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This report envisioned an extensive missile network buried beneath Greenland 's ice , spanning over 52,000 square miles -- three times the size of Denmark . <p> The design included deeply buried launch complexes and a sprawling network of tunnels intended to remain operational and unpredictable , with new tunnels excavated annually . Though ambitious , the full scope of Project Iceworm was not disclosed until decades after it was abandoned . <h> Camp Century 's structure and struggle to survive in the Arctic <p> Camp Century was a remarkable feat of engineering , established in 1959 through cut-and-cover trenching techniques . This Arctic subsurface camp comprised a network of parallel trenches housing various facilities and was designed to last 10 years with proper maintenance . Despite its ambitious design , the camp was manned for only 5 years and abandoned after 8 years . <p> The structural integrity of Camp Century faced significant challenges early on . The relentless pressure of the ice caused the trenches , including the largest that spanned 1,100 feet in length and stood 26 feet tall and wide , to succumb to vertical and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ continuous snow trimming to maintain functionality . The camp 's waste disposal systems , particularly the sewage system , also presented persistent problems . Located 150 feet from the nearest building , the initial lack of proper ventilation led to overpowering odors in the living quarters during the camp 's first year . Although venting improvements were made , they did not completely resolve the underlying issues . <p> By 1962 , core samples indicated that liquid waste had spread horizontally up to 170 feet , worsening the deformation of the trenches and the odors in the sleeping quarters . Camp Century provided substantial protection against the harsh Arctic conditions despite these challenges . <p> It boasted modern amenities , including bathrooms , dining areas , and medical facilities . The camp was also well-equipped with prefabricated buildings tucked neatly into the trenches , vehicles , and ample storage for fuel and food , demonstrating its capability to support its inhabitants in one of the planet 's most extreme environments . <h> Troubling tale of the PM-2A reactor <p> Camp Century was home to one of the first portable nuclear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ components small enough to be airlifted by a C-130 cargo plane . Despite its " portable " label at a hefty 330 tons , the reactor was an ambitious project . Dubbed the third of eight Army reactors , many of which were experimental attempts at portable nuclear power , the PM-2A 's operational history was fraught with challenges . <p> Installed in 1960 after being transported across Greenland 's icy expanses , the PM-2A was initially a beacon of fossil-fuel-free energy . However , it soon became notorious for its safety issues . The reactor was immediately shut down after reaching critical status due to neutron leakage . The Army 's makeshift solutions included lead shields and walls made of 55-gallon drums filled with ice and sawdust to protect against radiation . Nevertheless , the reactor operated for only two years , producing excessive stray neutrons and posing significant radiation hazards to personnel . <p> This neutron bombardment compromised the reactor 's structural integrity and contaminated the surrounding pristine Arctic environment . Traces of radioactive sodium were found in the snow , and cooling water leaks dispersed radioactive isotopes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ When the camp shut down in 1967 , the highly radioactive PM-2A was dismantled and buried in an Idaho nuclear waste dump , leaving behind unresolved concerns about its long-term environmental impact . <h> Hidden dangers resurface from Camp Century 's ice depths <p> In 2016 , a team of scientists revisiting the site of Camp Century delivered a stark warning . As climate change accelerates the melting of Greenland 's ice , the toxic remnants buried beneath -- radioactive cooling water , lead , fuel oil , and PCBs -- threaten to resurface by 2100 . This disturbing revelation has heightened diplomatic tensions among the United States , Denmark , and Greenland as they grapple with the daunting question of who is responsible for mitigating this potential environmental disaster . <p> The discovery underscores the long-term consequences of the Cold War 's secret endeavors , casting a shadow over the icy legacy of Camp Century . Despite the environmental risks , in October 1965 , the US Army optimistically declared subsurface ice camps like Camp Century feasible and advantageous due to the benefits of nuclear power . <p> Beyond @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ understanding of Earth 's ancient climate . Soil cores taken during its operation have proven invaluable . Analyzed with modern techniques , these cores have painted a picture of a once lush Greenland , teeming with mastodons , dense forests , and diverse wildlife . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> Recent surveys using NASA 's advanced radar technology in April 2024 have provided unprecedented detail of Camp Century 's layout . This technology , known as uninhabited aerial vehicle synthetic aperture radar , is crucial for mapping the internal layers of ice sheets and the bedrock below . Although Camp Century remains frozen for now , the potential for Greenland 's melting ice to expose its buried waste is a growing concern . <p> This rediscovery is not just a glimpse into covert military history but also a sobering reminder of the enduring impacts of military experimentation and nuclear projects . This not only makes the system more sustainable but also shows how food production can be made more environmentally friendly . <p> The broader implications of this research are profound . @@120206880 <p> Corals are fascinating marine organisms that are closely related to sea anemones and sea jellies . These soft-bodied animals are actually groups of tiny polyps , which can live individually or in large colonies , thus creating some of Earth 's most diverse and valuable ecosystems -- coral reefs . <p> Stony corals , also known as scleractinians , are the primary architects of these reef structures , secreting layers of calcium carbonate ( CaCO3 ) that gradually accumulate over centuries . With time , these calcium carbonate skeletons build up and create vast underwater networks that provide shelter , food , and breeding grounds for more than one million aquatic species . Research suggests that corals produce almost 9 lbs ( 4 kilograms ) of calcium carbonate per square meter per year , making them essential for supporting marine life . <p> However , the significance of corals extends beyond biodiversity , as their reefs serve as natural barriers against waves , storms , and floods , helping to prevent loss of life , property damage , and coastal erosion . They also safeguard shorelines by reducing the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ essential protection to coastal areas . Corals also play a great role in the oceans ' carbon cycling , helping to balance the acidity of seawater and maintain its chemical stability . Hence , they are undoubtedly integral to the health of our oceans . <p> Yet another remarkable fact about corals is their diverse reproductive strategies , with different species capable of reproducing through spawning , self-fertilization , or asexual reproduction . The most common method is spawning , during which corals release eggs and sperm into the water simultaneously in a highly synchronized event . While spawning relies on environmental cues such as temperature , lunar cycles , and daylight for success , recent findings reveal that the proximity of corals to one another is also a crucial factor . <p> The study , published in the peer-reviewed journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences ( PNAS ) , reveals that corals need to be practically neighbors to successfully reproduce . <h> Research insights <p> Led by Peter Mumby , PhD , a marine ecologist and a professorial research fellow at the University of Queensland , Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ just a few meters of each other for reproduction to occur effectively . This , according to Mumby , is hardly ideal in a world that 's heating up and bleaching them out of existence . <p> " It was surprising to see how close corals need to be -- within a few meters -- to have a high chance of success , " Mumby told Interesting Engineering ( IE ) in an interview . " We knew corals could n't be too far apart , but we found they need to be closer than we 'd expected . " <p> The reef research site in Nikko Bay , Palau , Micronesia . Source : Peter Mumby <p> Mumby explained that his interest in coral reproduction comes from the unique challenges of these stationary organisms . Since corals are sessile animals , meaning they can not move and are fixed in one place , they rely on being close to their neighbors for successful reproduction . During spawning , eggs from one coral must be fertilized by sperm from a nearby coral , making their proximity essential for reproduction . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be , " Mumby said , explaining that the team studied the success of a natural spawning event in Nikko Bay , in Micronesia 's Palau in March 2024 . " We measured the fertilization success of individual corals ( proportion of eggs fertilized ) and related this to neighborhood distances among corals . " <h> The discovery <p> To quantify reproduction success , the team set up egg collectors above 26 corals during the night of spawning . They then monitored the corals during the spawning event when the mostly hermaphroditic corals released eggs and sperm . " Once released ( as the corals spawn , which takes 15 minutes ) , the eggs can not escape but sperm is free to move in and out of the device , which floats on the sea surface , just like the free eggs do , " the scientist stated . " The containers captured some of each corals ' eggs and drifted to the surface where they followed the tide . " <p> " Although the eggs could not escape , sperm could enter the container and fertilize the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of drifting , the proportion of fertilized eggs was noted for each type of coral along with the distance to similarly established corals . " <p> Bundles of eggs are pushed up into the mouths of individual coral polyps , visible within 20 minutes before release ( spawning ) . Source : Peter Mumby <p> The team eventually found out that fertilization rates were highest , averaging 30% , when corals were in close proximity . However , these rates dropped to less than 10% at a distance of 10 meters and became virtually zero at 20 meters . " In what came as a surprise , we saw that corals needed to be within 10 meters of one another , and preferably closer than that for fertilization to take place , " Mumby added . <h> Addressing climate change impacts <p> Corals are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change , with rising ocean temperatures from global warming causing widespread coral bleaching . This phenomenon happens when they experience stress from prolonged heat and as a result , expel the algae ( zooxanthellae ) living within their tissues @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ become severely weakened . <p> " Climate change impacts like bleaching are killing and reducing the density of corals , so we 're concerned that individuals may end up too far apart to reproduce successfully , " Mumby pointed out . " This tells us how vulnerable coral populations become at low densities , so every effort must be taken to reduce the likelihood of that but when it does happen we should consider restoring the environment and corals appropriately . " <p> According to Christopher Doropoulos , PhD , a senior research scientist at the CSIRO , Australia 's national science agency , and co-author of the study , one approach is to give corals a bit of a push , helping them overcome the challenges posed by climate change and ensuring their reproduction continues successfully . <p> " In the future , we may need to help corals continue this key part of their lives , " Doropoulos said in a statement , adding that monitoring coral density at key locations and implementing restoration efforts to bring it back to levels needed for successful reproduction would be the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provides tangible targets for interventions like coral restoration . " <p> An egg holder drifting on the water surface with a night light attached . Source : Peter Mumby <p> Mumby observed that research indicated many corals may not be contributing to reproduction . " We also need to outplant corals close to neighbors ( within 5 meters ) , " he added . " Serious effects by reducing coral populations , which exacerbates the Allee effects as corals become further apart , but stress also reduces the number of eggs corals create . " <p> When asked about practical steps to address the issue of declining coral density in vulnerable regions , Mumby offered several suggestions . " Optimize reef management , such as reducing pollution and limiting fishing impacts , try to control pests like crown-of-thorns starfish . And if all that fails , restore corals back to required densities . " <p> But local communities and policymakers can also play a role in supporting coral restoration efforts . " They can create regulations that permit restoration within safe levels , " Mumby said . <p> Regarding the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he has been actively involved in efforts to repair damaged coral reefs . " Not all corals reproduce the same way , so we need to investigate these ideas in different types of coral , " he concluded . " Our work over the past 5 years on the Great Barrier Reef through the Reef Restoration and Adaptation Program is helping restoration practitioners set targets for density to help maintain coral populations . The case concerned an application to construct a wind farm in Co Laois . <p> An Bord Plean ? la rejected Planning Permission for the wind farm , citing the local development plan designation for wind turbines . Under the local County Development Plan in Laois , wind farms could not be constructed in the relevant area based on various criteria . <p> The developer sought to appeal the decision by way of judicial review before the High Court , arguing that Section 15(1) of the 2015 Act as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ obligations under the European Convention and Human Rights , that the Planning Authority had an obligation to interpret its planning decisions , such that climate considerations would take priority over the development plan and that the authority had therefore taken inadequate account of Section 15 of the Climate Act . <p> Section 15 of the Climate Act states that a relevant public body shall perform its functions in a manner consistent with the most recent approved Climate Action Plan , the most recent approved National Climate Action Strategy , the most recent National Adaptation Framework , and in furtherance of the National Climate Objective and the objective of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting the effects of climate change in the state . <p> In this particular case , 12 of the 13 proposed wind turbines were located in areas that were not open for consideration for wind farm development as per the Laois County Development Plan . <p> Accordingly , a Grant of Permission for the proposal then would have been a material contravention of the Laois County Development Plan and its associated wind energy strategy . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ permission be refused on the basis that the proposed development would be identified as material contravention and consequently was contrary to proper planning and sustainable development in the area . <p> The developer applied for judicial review , seeking certiorari quashing the decision of the board . The principal grounds of the challenge was that the board had erred in law in failing to comply with its obligations under Section 15 of the Climate Action and Low Cabon Development Act 2015 . The submissions essentially were that the board had failed to carry out its functions insofar as practicable with the Climate Action Plan . <p> Mr Justice Humphreys , the judge who dealt with the case in the High Court , undertook a detailed consideration of the interpretation of Section 15 of the 2015 Act and summarised the board 's obligations under Section 15 , which was when making a decision it had to be relevant to the achievement of the climate objectives . <p> The court found that the board failed to exercise its power in a manner compliant with the Climate Objectives and policies set out in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there was a breach of duty under the European Court of Human Rights Legislation and other European law . <p> The court granted the application for judicial review and ordered that the application be remitted to An Bord Plean ? la for further consideration in accordance with the Judgement . <p> This is a significant case and places obligations on public bodies , particularly planning bodies , in respect of renewable energy developments and indicates that such state bodies will have to factor in Climate Objectives before making decisions , and this certainly will have significant impacts or repercussions on the renewable energy sector for wind and solar developers who are bringing planning applications to construct solar or wind farms , particularly on agricultural lands . <p> Stephen Coppinger is a solicitor practising in Walsh &amp; Partners , Solicitors and Commissioners for Oaths , 17 , South Mall , Cork . @@120240663 <h> ' Catastrophe bonds ' may offset LA wildfire damage , part of a perverse trade in dystopia <h> Buyers can purchase shares in how likely it is that 2025 will be the hottest year on record or if a nuclear weapon will detonate soon <p> More than 25,000 acres were burned during recent wildfires that spread across LA . The ashes have n't settled but the LA fires show that traditional insurance is over because catastrophe is always coming . Photograph : Mario Tama/Getty Images <p> Rachel O'Dwyer <p> Mon Jan 20 2025 - 06:00 <p> The Pacific Palisades neighbourhood , situated between the Santa Monica mountains and the Pacific Ocean , had one of the most expensive real estate markets in Los Angeles . These properties were also extremely hard to insure because of the risk of wildfires . The surrounding region had dry vegetation that was ideal kindling after the hottest summer on record . The seasonal Santa Ana winds spread flames rapidly . Luxury properties were built into the hills off the Pacific Coast highway , often on secluded roads that are hard to access in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ State Farm revoked 1,600 existing policies . Many residents now do n't know where they stand . The LA wildfires are unusual in that affluent neighbourhoods have been most affected . The effects of climate destruction normally skew towards poorer communities . Forty per cent of people in the United States are now living in areas at high risk of property damage and destruction from climate change . <p> Climate change has become uninsurable -- at least by typical parameters . That 's where catastrophe bonds come in . The " cat bond " , as it 's known , is a speculative financial instrument for managing unmanageable risk . Traditional insurers will offset this risk in their portfolios -- from a natural disaster or cataclysmic event -- to agents known as reinsurers ( companies that provide insurance to insurers . Then there are retrocessionaires , who provide insurance to reinsurers . Thankfully the process stops here . ) Insurance companies will increasingly rely on these reinsurers to help pay for disasters like the Californian wildfires , which some estimate could cost as much as $275 billion . Ireland currently @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reinsurers . <p> In the 1990s insurers in Florida were bankrupted by damage from Hurricane Andrew . Afterwards it was nearly impossible for Florida residents to get home insurance . Traditional insurance models collapsed in the face of a systemic risk they were unable to absorb . Catastrophe bonds were born . The bond is a bet on a cataclysmic event like a storm , typhoon or hurricane that causes devastating damage to property . And in doing so they package the unworkable risk of climate change into a speculative instrument . <p> If the event happens the bond is triggered and a payout is made . If it does n't the issuer gets their initial investment back -- with interest . But how this " happening " is measured for the purposes of a payout is Byzantine in its complexity . <p> In developed countries measuring involves a threshold of on-the-ground damage . In underdeveloped nations , however , where cat bonds are often the main insurance against climate catastrophe , it 's less straightforward . These are places such as the Caribbean , Latin American countries and parts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , facing significant climate risk and unable to afford insurance premiums . The IMF and the World Bank now recommends catastrophe bonds as the insurance solution to climate change adaptation for such nations . Here a bond is triggered not by estimated damage , which takes time to assess and remunerate , but through meteorological data . <p> In 2021 Jamaica purchased a cat bond through the World Banks 's capital-at-risk programme . In 2024 the country was hit by Hurricane Beryl as it swept towards the Cayman Islands . Despite doing widespread damage barometric readings were 9 millibars off the level needed to trigger the payout . Investors made a killing from Beryl . <p> A similar story occurred in 2014 when Storm Odile struck Mexico , causing an estimated $1.22 billion damage . Pressure readings were hampered by the storm itself ; some weather stations had even been barricaded to protect them from damage . The definitive reading of 943.1 millibars was taken by Josh Morgerman , an amateur storm chaser from West Hollywood , just shy of the 930 millibar reading ( air pressure drops as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the storm is an indication of its strength ) necessary for a $50 million payout . In a letter to the LA Times , Morgerman likened it to using temperature readings to trigger a fire-insurance claim . " Who cares how hot it was ? The house burned down . " <p> The catastrophe bond trades in states of exception , but where climate change is concerned , the exceptional is now the norm . And there are markets for this perpetual state of disaster capitalism . <p> Go to Polymarket , a kind of futures market for betting on , well , futures , and you can stake any dystopia you believe may soon be reality . Buyers can purchase shares in how likely it is that 2025 will be the hottest year on record , whether a nuclear weapon will detonate soon and if the doomsday clock , a man-made indicator of how close we are to self-destruction , will move closer to midnight . <p> The ashes have n't settled , but the LA fires show that traditional insurance is over because catastrophe is always coming . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with a crisis that affects us all but which costs vulnerable communities so much more ? In What Money Ca n't Buy , Michael Sandel explores the moral conundrum of selling " goods " such as superior healthcare , organs , and the right to pollute -- which is to say , he debates the morality of turning these things into an economic good in the first place . Is it okay , for example , to purchase a " viatical " -- a share in a life insurance policy that yields a profit when the claimant dies ? In the late1990s , as the Aids pandemic shifted from a fatal disease that governments were unwilling to account for to a chronic illness , some survivors got calls from brokers who had bought their policies for a killing , asking why they were n't dead yet . <p> Through the lens of trading instruments the cat bond or the viatical is just another bet . It does n't matter if it wagers on death , global pandemic or environmental catastrophe . <p> " Market think " is so invisible it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ call it perverse . This market turns shared disaster into a profitable bet . Instead of recognising our collective fate in the climate crisis it offsets risk on to the most vulnerable , when the cost was never theirs to assume . <p> Rachel O'Dwyer is a writer and lecturer in digital cultures in the National College of Art and Design , Dublin

@@120240975 <p> A chain of unexplained rings rises from the Sunbury hills at the fringe of Melbourne , Australia . These earth rings , located in Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Country , are not a natural formation but evidence of human effort . <p> Showing Ancient Aboriginal people and their ongoing connection to the Country , these structures depict the landscape 's cultural and spiritual significance . <p> A new study combines the first archaeological excavation of one of the rings with the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung knowledge . This achievement increases the knowledge of Australia 's archaeological tradition , which covers over 65,000 years of continuous occupation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples . <h> Secret sites of ceremony <p> Across the world , in places such as the Amazon , England , and Cambodia , ancient ceremonial sites exist in the form of earth rings . These rings were created hundreds , if not thousands , of years ago , by carving out dirt into circular shapes that were hundreds of meters wide . <p> In Australia 's east , earth rings are categorized as sacred ceremonial sites for Aboriginal language groups @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ colonization and land development . Hundreds used to exist throughout New South Wales and Queensland , but there are merely 100 of them left today . In Victoria , five earth rings , including the Sunbury rings , have been reported . <p> Sunbury earth rings are significant to the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung people and their heritage , the original inhabitants of a large stretch in central-southern Victoria . The terrain provides evidence of people living , coexisting , and creating generations , as well as the perpetual cycle of defiance against occupation by foreign forces . <p> The Wurundjeri Woi-Wurrung conducted a cultural values study of the region encompassing the Sunbury rings during 2021-2022 . This area has continued to be managed and restored using traditional lore and beliefs associated with ancestors Bunjil and Waa . Moreover , the Narrap team actively participates in the preservation of the cultural and ecological well-being of this area . <h> Revisiting the Sunbury Ring G <p> In 2022 , the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung people performed an archaeological dig at Sunbury Ring G , a place of cultural and ceremonial significance . This site , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , separated by Jacksons Creek , was previously excavated in 1979 by archaeologist David Frankel . <p> 166 stone artifacts were examined as part of this new research . The deposits were dated while the artifacts were reconstructed . All of this brought to light the methods and tools used by the people of Woi-Wurrung . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> The study of the Sunbury Ring G suggests that it was built at a time period ranging from 590 to 1,400 years ago . So , the builders probably went to a nearby forest , cleared the land , and built the ring . Additionally , they created stone tools , processed several plants and animals , and set up campfires at the location . <p> Some wear patterns on certain artifacts indicate they served ceremonial purposes , such as the crafting of feather ornaments and scarification , which had been practiced and reported in other regions of Victoria . <p> This research is the first of its kind and represents the collage of the archaeological and cultural interpretation of Australian earth rings . @@120241056 <p> As awareness of veganism has increased , the more UPFs have proliferated , meaning that a lifestyle based on the consumption of natural whole foods and plants has moved ever further away from veganism 's original philosophy . <p> Why Veganism ? <p> Veganism is a lifestyle philosophy , meaning it touches not just food and drink , but the things we buy to use , to clothe , to furnish our homes with ; even the way we move and travel . The pillar familiar to most concerns food and drink , with many reasons why people opt into veganism . <p> The main reason is a fundamental disagreement with the consumption of animals and animal products . Another is the perception that a vegan diet is healthier than one that includes consumption of meat , etc . Other reasons include health/wellbeing , environmental concerns including the impact of animal agriculture on climate change , and religious or spiritual beliefs . <p> These reasons are not held in a perfectly balanced ratio but slip and slide depending on the individual . <p> At its core , veganism has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ prioritise to eat . <p> The problems come when there is a drastic change in diet without the proper know-how or experience to replace the vital nutrients , vitamins and minerals provided by meat , fish and dairy that our bodies need to function well . <p> Health <p> First , if you 're thinking about going vegan , it 's advisable to get a health check from your GP , including bloods , for two reasons . It ensures you are not deficient in any vitamin or mineral , ( e.g. , low iron count ) , that could be exacerbated by , e.g. , taking red meat out of your diet . If all is well , it provides a picture of your base level of health and function for the future as you adapt to a new way of eating . <p> Vitamin B12 , iron and calcium are three vital minerals that are concentrated in animal products . They are also present in myriad natural plant-based foods , but more of those foods may need to be consumed to get your quotient to maintain levels over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ health issues including fatigue , organ failure and brittle bones . <p> Eat Food , Not Too Much , Mostly Plants <p> The food philosopher , Michael Pollan , coined this famous triptych in his book The Omnivore 's Dilemma . Clearly , this is not a strict food rule for vegans but is a good guiding principle , important for a healthy vegan diet because it excludes UPFs for everyone . <p> Plant-based does not simply mean no ingredient of animal origin . It does mean a diet made up of natural wholefoods , including vegetables , fruits , flowers and seaweeds , legumes ( peas , beans and lentils ) , grains , nuts and seeds . <p> The NOVA food classification system was developed in 2009 as " a framework for grouping edible substances based on the extent and purpose of food processing applied to them " . <p> A food is classified as a UPF if it has five or more ingredients in its make-up and uses ingredients not typically used in home cooking . <p> Such ingredients are " preservatives , flavour enhancers , colourings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ taste and longer shelf life . " <p> Not all such ingredients are ' bad -- for example , seaweed can be used as an emulsifier as can seed oils , and salt and vinegar are essential ingredients in pickles and ferments , techniques used to preserve and extend the life of fresh foods . <p> But their overuse , particularly in convenience foods , pushes the boundary of what a plant-based food is . Therefore , just because a product says it 's vegan , does n't make it healthy or better for you than a conventional convenience food product , like beer-battered onion rings . <p> Get to Know Your Greengrocer <p> Greengrocers are small businesses that specialise in sourcing and growing seasonal vegetables and fruits . @@120241651 <h> We live in what feels like dark and anxious times -- but there 's still lots we can learn from the stars <p> The stars ' silent message is that our sparkling blue marble is a preciously rare home in the immensity of space <p> by : Roberto Trotta <p> 19 Jan 2025 <p> Illustration : Big Issue <p> Share <p> American naturalist William Beebe , considered one of the founders of ecology , tells of an astronomical rite he used to follow with colonel Roosevelt in his home on Long Island . After an evening of discussions " around the fringes of knowledge " , Beebe and the future president of the United States would go out into the night and search for the Andromeda galaxy , a smudge of light easily missed even in the utterly dark skies of the 1890s , and the most distant object in the universe visible with the naked eye . <p> When they had contemplated Andromeda at some length , one of them would recite : <p> That is the spiral galaxy of Andromeda.It is as large as our Milky Way.It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ away.It consists of one hundred billion suns , each larger than our sun . <p> What would we lose if we could not stargaze ? Or indeed , what did we lose , now that the " perpetual presence of the sublime " , as Emerson called the stars , is hidden by the orange haze of light pollution for most of us ? <p> To understand the role that the stars have played in the making of our species , we must imagine how different we would be had we been fated to live on a planet without stars -- one covered in clouds everywhere and all the time . Without a clear sight of the night sky , our ancestors would not have been able to use the stars for navigating , both overland like native peoples of Australia used to do , nor across the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean , where Polynesian master navigators regularly undertook the 4,000-miles-long trip between New Zealand and Tahiti . <p> Without the phases of the moon following a 29.5-days long cycle , ancient calendars -- all moon-based -- would @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 17,000 years ago featuring 29 human-made notches appears to be one of the very first such time-keeping devices , which might have been used to keep track of both the moon and the female cycle at the same time . This would make of women not only the first astronomers , but also the first mathematicians . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Without the maddening irregular movement of the planets ( from a Greek word that means " wanderer " ) to puzzle about , we would not have had astrology , responsible not only for naming the days of the week we still use today , but also for thousands of years of obsessive observation of the sky . All of this neck-craning awe would then fuel the scientific revolution of the 17th century , when astronomy was born out of astrology , and would become the midwife of science , giving rise to modern physics as we know it . <p> But the night sky gave us more than all the science and technology that underpin our lives today . Spirituality and religious beliefs were often defined by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were thought to reside . Even our mysterious supremacy over the Neanderthals who had roamed across Europe for hundreds of thousands of years before our ancestors trotted out of Africa 50,000 years ago , might have been gained thanks to a secret weapon hidden in plain sight above their heads . The night sky might have offered star-savvy Homo sapiens crucial evolutionary advantage over our Neanderthal cousins , thus sealing their fate and propelling us towards today 's star-driven planetary domination . <p> We now live in what often feels like dark and anxious times . Accelerating climate change , vast loss of biodiversity , increasing political polarisation and terrible conflicts threaten our survival , and that of the planet , because of the very technology that the stars helped us bring forth . Some are turning to the stars as an escape hatch , in the hope of colonising Mars and from there , one day , the galaxy . But their plans are delusional : there is no planet B , and the prospect of leaving an ecologically compromised Earth behind is not only technologically unfeasible , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the stars for a different kind of inspiration . In recapturing the sense of awe and wonder that our ancestors experienced under dark skies , and in contemplating our smallness in the vastness of an inhospitable cosmos , like Teddy Roosevelt used to do , we have a potent antidote to the hubris that has led us to the brink of self-destruction . <p> Let the stars speak to us once again . Their silent message , connecting us to all generations of humans , is that our sparkling blue marble is a preciously rare home in the immensity of space . It is high time for us to become good ancestors , and take better care of Earth , the only home we 'll ever have .

@@120283312 <h> Is hydrogen the future for cars ? Manufacturers have n't given up on it yet <p> Announcing the 2028 launch of its first hydrogen-powered fuel-cell electric car ( FCEV ) -- the iX5 Hydrogen -- last year , BMW described hydrogen cars as the ' missing piece ' in the sustainable mobility jigsaw . And it 's easy to understand the excitement . On paper fuel cell cars have all the environmental benefits of battery electric vehicles ( BEVs ) with the added perk that they can be fuelled in three to four minutes . <p> But while BMW and several other car manufacturers remain optimistic that hydrogen will be the next big thing for greener motoring , others think that the race has already been run . <p> ' Ten years ago , it was a reasonable question to ask would the future of decarbonised road transport involve hydrogen ? ' says Frank Hodgson , a senior energy analyst at Regen , who provides independent energy systems expertise to assist the UK 's journey to net zero . ' But we 've proven since then that the powertrain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . ' We are n't seeing sales of hydrogen cars at all .
